codebook_metadata.title: Existential Analysis & Logotherapy Four Fundamental Motivations (4FMs) Codebook
codebook_metadata.purpose: Interpretive thematic analysis of therapeutic intervention participant testimony
codebook_metadata.methodology: Thematic analysis using 4FMs as primary domains
codebook_metadata.copyright: ©2026 Aestra Inc. except when external source noted.

sources.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

theoretical_foundation.description: Four fundamental structures or 'cornerstones of existence' that require continuous dialogical confrontation and exchange
theoretical_foundation.source_quote: All preconditions of existence can be summarized in four fundamental structures, the 'cornerstones of existence': the world in its factuality and potentiality; life with its network of relationships and its feelings; being oneself as a unique, autonomous person; the wider context where to place oneself = development through one's activities, opening one's future

conceptual_basis.description: Motivation emerges from dialogical exchange between subject and environment
conceptual_basis.source_quote: Motivation is a process of continuous exchange between the subject—individual—and the environment. From an existential perspective, we see this exchange as having a dialogical structure, connecting the given reality of both subject and object with the intentions of the individual.

FM1_world.name: First Fundamental Motivation: The World
FM1_world.subtitle: Dealing with Conditions and Possibilities
FM1_world.description: Confrontation with the factuality and potentiality of the world; the foundation of existence
FM1_world.source_quote: the world in its factuality and potentiality

existential_question.question: I am—can I be?
existential_question.practical_application: Can I claim my place in this world under the conditions and with the possibilities I have?
existential_question.source_quote: I am—can I be? For making this question practical, I may apply it to my own situation. Then I may ask myself: Can I claim my place in this world under the conditions and with the possibilities I have?

existential_needs.verification_question: Do I enjoy protection, acceptance, do I feel at home somewhere?
existential_needs.source_quote: This demands three things: protection, space and support.—Do I enjoy protection, acceptance, do I feel at home somewhere?

existential_needs.description: Having enough space for being there
existential_needs.verification_question: Do I have enough space for being there?
existential_needs.source_quote: This demands three things: protection, space and support.—Do I enjoy protection, acceptance, do I feel at home somewhere?—Do I have enough space for being there?

existential_needs.verification_question: Where do I find support in my life?
existential_needs.source_quote: This demands three things: protection, space and support.—Do I enjoy protection, acceptance, do I feel at home somewhere?—Do I have enough space for being there?—Where do I find support in my life?

positive_outcomes.description: Confidence in oneself and possibly faith in God
positive_outcomes.source_quote: But if I do have these three things, I will be able to feel trust in the world and confidence in myself, maybe even faith in God.

positive_outcomes.description: Trust in whatever one feels as being the last support in life
positive_outcomes.source_quote: The sum of these experiences of trust is the fundamental trust, the trust in whatever I feel as being the last support in my life.

negative_outcomes.source_quote: If this is not the case, the result will be restlessness, insecurity and fear
If this is not the case, the result will be restlessness, insecurity and fear
If this is not the case, the result will be restlessness, insecurity and fear

action_accept.description: Being ready to occupy space, rely on support, and trust protection
action_accept.source_quote: To accept means to be ready to occupy the space, to rely on the support and to trust the protection; in short 'to be there' and not to flee.

action_endure.description: The force to let be whatever is difficult, menacing or unalterable
action_endure.source_quote: To endure means the force to let be whatever is difficult, menacing or unalterable and to 'support' what cannot be changed.

coping_reactions.description: Psychodynamics that secure life when acceptance is not possible
coping_reactions.source_quote: If this is not the case, psychodynamics takes over the guidance in the form of coping reactions, which are to secure life

FM2_life.name: Second Fundamental Motivation: Life
FM2_life.subtitle: Dealing with Relationships and Emotions
FM2_life.description: Confrontation with the network of relationships and feelings; the pathic dimension of existence
FM2_life.source_quote: life with its network of relationships and its feelings

pathic_dimension.description: Existence is experienced and suffered or enjoyed, not simply happening
pathic_dimension.source_quote: It has a 'pathic dimension,' which means that it does not simply happen, but that we experience and suffer or enjoy it.

existential_question.question: I am alive—do I like this fact?
existential_question.alternative_form: Is it good to be there?
existential_question.source_quote: Therefore, I am confronted with the fundamental question of life: I am alive—do I like this fact? Is it good to be there?

existential_needs.description: Having relationships where one feels closeness and community
existential_needs.verification_question: Do I have relationships, in which I feel closeness, for which I spend time and in which I experience community?
existential_needs.source_quote: In order to seize my life, to love it, I need three things: relationship, time and closeness.—In verifying the presence of life in one's own situation we may ask ourselves questions like this: Do I have relationships, in which I feel closeness, for which I spend time and in which I experience community?

existential_needs.description: Taking time for valuable things, giving away part of one's life
existential_needs.verification_question: What do I take time for? Do I take time for valuable things, worthy to spend my time for?
existential_needs.source_quote: What do I take time for? Do I take time for valuable things, worthy to spend my time for? To take time for something means to give away a part of one's life while spending it with someone or something.

existential_needs.description: Feeling and maintaining closeness to things, plants, animals, and people
existential_needs.verification_question: Can I feel close and maintain closeness to things, plants, animals and people? Can I admit the closeness of someone else?
existential_needs.source_quote: Can I feel close and maintain closeness to things, plants, animals and people? Can I admit the closeness of someone else?

positive_outcomes.description: Experience of being in harmony with the world and oneself
positive_outcomes.source_quote: But if these three conditions are fulfilled, I experience myself as being in harmony with the world and with myself, and I can sense the depth of life.

positive_outcomes.description: Most profound feeling for the value of life; yardstick for all emotions
positive_outcomes.source_quote: These experiences form the fundamental value, the most profound feeling for the value of life. In each experience of a value this fundamental value is touched upon; it colors the emotions and affects and represents our yardstick for anything we might feel to be of worth.

negative_outcomes.source_quote: If relationships, closeness and time are lacking, longing will arise, then coldness and finally depression.
If relationships, closeness and time are lacking, longing will arise, then coldness and finally depression.
If relationships, closeness and time are lacking, longing will arise, then coldness and finally depression.

action_turn_to.description: Turning toward people, things, animals, work, or oneself; getting close and making contact
action_turn_to.source_quote: I seize life, engage in it, when I turn to other people, to things, animals, intellectual work or to myself, when I go towards it, get close, get into touch or pull it towards me.

grief_process.description: Grief arises when turning to a loss
grief_process.source_quote: If I turn to a loss, grief arises.

consent_to_feeling.description: Consent to being touched for life to move freely within
consent_to_feeling.source_quote: If life is to make me move freely, my consent to being touched (to feeling) is necessary.

FM3_being_person.name: Third Fundamental Motivation: Being a Person
FM3_being_person.subtitle: Dealing with Uniqueness and Conscience
FM3_being_person.description: Confrontation with one's uniqueness as an autonomous person; the plane of identity and ethics
FM3_being_person.source_quote: being oneself as a unique, autonomous person

existential_question.question: I am myself—may I be like this?
existential_question.alternative_form: Do I feel free to be like that? Do I have the right to be what I am and to behave as I do?
existential_question.context: The plane of identity, of knowing oneself and of ethics
existential_question.source_quote: In the midst of this world, I discover myself unmistakably; I am with myself and I am given to myself. This puts before me the fundamental question of being a person: I am myself—may I be like this? Do I feel free to be like that? Do I have the right to be what I am and to behave as I do?—This is the plane of identity, of knowing oneself and of ethics.

existential_needs.description: Being seen; having one's uniqueness considered
existential_needs.verification_question: By whom am I seen? Who considers my uniqueness and respects my boundaries?
existential_needs.source_quote: In order to succeed here, it is necessary to have experienced three things: attention, justice and appreciation.—Again, one can verify this third cornerstone of existence in one's own existence by asking: by whom am I seen? Who considers my uniqueness and respects my boundaries?

existential_needs.verification_question: For what am I appreciated—for what can I appreciate myself?
existential_needs.source_quote: For what am I appreciated—for what can I appreciate myself?

positive_outcomes.source_quote: If, on the contrary, these experiences have been made, I will find myself; find my authenticity, my relief and my self-respect.

positive_outcomes.description: Experience of relief in being oneself
positive_outcomes.source_quote: If, on the contrary, these experiences have been made, I will find myself; find my authenticity, my relief and my self-respect.
If, on the contrary, these experiences have been made, I will find myself; find my authenticity, my relief and my self-respect.

positive_outcomes.description: Profoundest worth identifying one's own self at its core
positive_outcomes.source_quote: The sum of these experiences builds one's own worth, the profoundest worth of what identifies my own self at its core: the self-esteem.

negative_outcomes.source_quote: If these experiences are missing, solitude will be the result, hysteria as well as a need to hide behind the shame.
If these experiences are missing, solitude will be the result, hysteria as well as a need to hide behind the shame.
If these experiences are missing, solitude will be the result, hysteria as well as a need to hide behind the shame.

action_encounter.description: Looking at others, encountering them; finding their essence and one's own 'I' in the 'you'
action_encounter.source_quote: Encounter and regret are the two means by which we can live our authenticity without ending up in solitude. Encounter represents the necessary bridge to the other, makes me find his essence as well as my own 'I' in the 'you.'

action_demarcate.description: Demarcating oneself and standing by one's own
action_demarcate.source_quote: This requires my active participation: to look at other people, to encounter them and, at the same time, to demarcate myself and to stand by my own, but to refuse whatever does not correspond to me.

action_regret.description: Regret as means to live authenticity
action_regret.source_quote: Encounter and regret are the two means by which we can live our authenticity without ending up in solitude.

FM4_meaning.name: Fourth Fundamental Motivation: Meaning
FM4_meaning.subtitle: Dealing with Becoming, Future and Commitment
FM4_meaning.description: Confrontation with the wider context for placing oneself; development through activities and opening one's future
FM4_meaning.source_quote: the wider context where to place oneself = development through one's activities, opening one's future

existential_question.question: I am there—for what is it good?
existential_question.context: Recognition of what life is all about; need to transcend oneself for fulfillment
existential_question.source_quote: If I can be there, love life and find myself therein, the conditions are fulfilled for the fourth fundamental condition of existence: the recognition of what my life is all about. It does not suffice to simply be there and to have found oneself. In a sense, we have to transcend ourselves, if we want to find fulfillment and to be fruitful... Thus, the transience of life puts before us the question of meaning of our existence: I am there—for what is it good?

existential_needs.description: A place where one feels needed and can be productive
existential_needs.verification_question: Is there a place where I feel needed, where I can be productive?
existential_needs.source_quote: For this, three things are necessary: a field of activity, a structural context and a value to be realized in the future.—For a practical application, we can ask ourselves questions of the following type: is there a place where I feel needed, where I can be productive?

existential_needs.description: A larger context providing structure and orientation to life
existential_needs.verification_question: Do I see and experience myself in a larger context that provides structure and orientation to my life? Where I want to be integrated?
existential_needs.source_quote: Do I see and experience myself in a larger context that provides structure and orientation to my life? Where I want to be integrated?

existential_needs.need: Value to be realized in future
existential_needs.description: Something that should still be realized in one's life
existential_needs.verification_question: Is there anything that should still be realized in my life?
existential_needs.source_quote: Is there anything that should still be realized in my life?

positive_outcomes.source_quote: If, on the contrary, these conditions are met, I will be capable of dedication and action and, finally, of my own form of religious belief.
If, on the contrary, these conditions are met, I will be capable of dedication and action and, finally, of my own form of religious belief.

positive_outcomes.description: One's own form of religious belief
positive_outcomes.source_quote: If, on the contrary, these conditions are met, I will be capable of dedication and action and, finally, of my own form of religious belief.

positive_outcomes.description: Sense of fulfillment; sum of meaningful experiences
positive_outcomes.source_quote: The sum of these experiences adds up to the meaning of life and leads to a sense of fulfillment.

negative_outcomes.source_quote: If this is not the case, the result will be a feeling of emptiness, frustration, even despair and frequently addiction.
If this is not the case, the result will be a feeling of emptiness, frustration, even despair and frequently addiction.
If this is not the case, the result will be a feeling of emptiness, frustration, even despair and frequently addiction.
If this is not the case, the result will be a feeling of emptiness, frustration, even despair and frequently addiction.

phenomenological_attitude.description: Attitude of openness; dealing with questions in each situation
phenomenological_attitude.source_quote: But it does not suffice to have a field of activity, to have one's place within a context and to know of values to be realized in the future. Instead, the phenomenological attitude is needed, which we spoke about at the beginning. This attitude of openness represents the existential access to meaning in life: i.e., dealing with the questions put before me in each situation

dialogical_questioning.description: What does this hour want from me, how shall I respond?
dialogical_questioning.source_quote: 'What does this hour want from me, how shall I respond?' The meaningful thing is not only what I can expect from life, but, in accordance with the dialogical structure of existence, it is equally important what life wants from me and what the moment expects from me and what I could and should do now for others as well as for myself.

action_agreement.description: Bringing oneself into agreement with the situation; examining if actions are good
action_agreement.source_quote: My active part in this attitude of openness is to bring myself into agreement with the situation, to examine whether what I am doing is really a good thing: for others, for myself, for the future, for my environment. If I act accordingly, my existence will be fulfilling.

existential_meaning.description: The most valuable, realistic possibility of the given situation, for which one feels one should decide
existential_meaning.source_quote: This notion of valuable possibilities endorsed with the theory of the fundamental existential motivations, defines meaning even more concretely as 'the most valuable, realistic possibility of the given situation, for which I feel I should decide myself.'

frankl_definition.description: A possibility against the background of reality
frankl_definition.source_quote: Viktor Frankl (1987, p. 315) once defined meaning as 'a possibility against the background of reality.'

ontological_meaning.description: Overall meaning independent of the individual; philosophical and religious meaning
ontological_meaning.source_quote: Besides this existential meaning, there is an ontological meaning. This is the overall meaning in which I find myself and which does not depend on me. It is the philosophical and religious meaning, the meaning the creator of the world must have had in mind.

steps.name: Recognizing
steps.description: Recognizing something in its worth or value, as it speaks to us
steps.source_quote: Recognizing something in its worth or value, insofar as it speaks to us. This is often a challenge demanding action on our part. To see what a situation provokes in us means to recognize the situational meaning involved.

steps.name: Harmonizing
steps.description: Bringing perceived value into accordance with inner reality
steps.source_quote: Harmonizing. Bringing the perceived value, challenge or meaning into accordance with one's inner reality, i.e., examining the consistency with the rest of our values, with attitudes, abilities and capabilities and with our conscience.

steps.name: Inner consent
steps.description: Inner consent to one's own active involvement, bringing presence of the inner person
steps.source_quote: The final step in the development of motivation is the inner consent to one's own active involvement. This consent and the act of harmonizing the new value with inner (already existing personal) reality leads to the presence of the inner person in one's actions. It brings up the integration of the new value and the person himself into a wider context (meaning).

structure_of_will.description: Free and realistic will based on fundamental elements

elements.description: Real ability and capacity of the subject
elements.source_quote: on the real ability and capacity of the subject

elements.description: Emotional perception of the situational value
elements.source_quote: on the emotional perception of the situational value

elements.description: Inner permission for action from agreement with life concepts and morality
elements.source_quote: on the inner permission for that act, emerging from an agreement with one's concepts of life and morality

elements.description: Meaning as the moving part in free will (Frankl's contribution)
elements.source_quote: Frankl (1970, pp. 37-44; 1987, pp. 101-104) saw meaning as the moving part in free will.

coding_guidelines.application: Use this codebook to identify and code participant testimony related to the four fundamental motivations
coding_guidelines.hierarchical_structure: Code using FM1-FM4 as primary domains, with sub-codes for needs, outcomes, and actions
coding_guidelines.temporal_analysis: Consider participant experiences before, during, and after therapeutic intervention
coding_guidelines.exclusion_criteria: Only code content that directly relates to the described themes with supporting evidence from source materials

version_notes.v3.0: Initial codebook based on Längle (2011). Includes all four fundamental motivations with existential questions, needs, positive/negative outcomes, active participation elements, motivational process steps, and structure of will.
